How to connect your marketing to booked jobs

A practical look at the systems between a lead and a paid invoice, and where most service businesses lose opportunities.

Savvy Team Growth strategy · Savvy Post Marketing

Where the leads actually go

Most owners we talk to can tell you what they spend on marketing each month. Far fewer can tell you how many of last month’s booked jobs came from that spend. The gap isn’t a reporting problem. It’s a systems problem: somewhere between the first ring and the paid invoice, the trail goes cold.

Picture a typical week. Ads and search bring in, say, 120 calls and form fills. Some are existing customers, some are vendors, a few are wrong numbers. Of the real opportunities, some go to voicemail, some get a quote that nobody follows up on, and some book a job that never gets tagged with where it came from. By Friday, the marketing looks expensive and nobody can say exactly why.

“A campaign can create a lead and still fail to create revenue.”

The fix is not more leads. It’s making sure the leads you already pay for can be followed from source to invoice. That takes four steps, in this order.

Step 1 · Track every lead to a source

If you can’t say where a job came from, you can’t decide where to spend the next dollar. Source tracking doesn’t need to be complicated, but it does need to be consistent across every channel and every person who answers the phone.

  • Call tracking numbers per channel
  • Form source captured in the CRM
  • One “how did you hear about us” field, used consistently

The last point matters more than it looks. When the office manager writes “Google”, a technician writes “internet” and the owner writes “LSA”, you end up with three sources that are really one. Pick a short list of options, make it a required dropdown, and review it monthly.

Step 2 · Answer faster than the competition

Homeowners with a problem tend to call down a list. If you don’t answer, the next company on the list probably will. Speed to answer is the cheapest lead-generation tool most service businesses have, and it’s almost never in the marketing budget.

Start by measuring it. Most phone systems and call-tracking tools can show missed calls by hour of the day. Look for the patterns: lunch breaks, early mornings, Saturdays, the half hour after dispatch meetings. Those windows are where paid demand quietly leaks away.

In practice · HVAC

After-hours calls routed to an answering service, with a same-morning callback list for anything not booked overnight.

Step 3 · Follow up on every estimate

An estimate is not a lost job until the customer says no. Yet in many businesses, an estimate that isn’t signed on the spot simply disappears. Nobody owns the follow-up, so nobody does it.

A simple cadence works better than heroic effort: a thank-you the same day, a check-in call two days later, and a final note a week after that. Put it in the CRM as tasks, assign an owner, and track how many open estimates get a second touch.

A simple estimate follow-up cadence (example)
WhenChannelPurpose
Same dayText or emailThank them, recap the options, make it easy to say yes
Day 2Phone callAnswer questions, handle the real objection
Day 7EmailLast check-in, offer to revisit timing or scope
Day 30EmailSeasonal reminder or financing option, then close the loop

Step 4 · Report on revenue, not clicks

Once leads carry a source and estimates have an owner, reporting gets much more useful. Instead of clicks and impressions, the monthly report can answer the questions an owner actually asks: which channels produced booked jobs, what those jobs were worth, and what it cost to win them.

You don’t need a perfect attribution model to get there. A spreadsheet that joins “source” from the CRM with “invoice total” from your field-service software is enough to start making better decisions next month.

What to do this month

Pick one step and finish it before starting the next. For most teams that means cleaning up lead sources first, because every other improvement depends on being able to see it.

  1. Audit the “lead source” field in your CRM and collapse it to a short, required list.
  2. Pull missed-call data for the last 30 days and find your two worst time windows.
  3. Assign an owner to every open estimate and schedule a second touch.
  4. Build one simple report that ends with booked revenue by source.

Key takeaways

  • Most leads are lost between the call and the estimate, not in the ads.
  • Track every lead to a source before spending more on demand.
  • Response time and estimate follow-up are the two highest-leverage fixes.
  • A good report ends with revenue, not clicks.
